Admonish
ad-MON-ish
verb (ministry; mutual duty)
From Latin admonere, to put in mind, to warn; rendering Greek noutheteo, to place in the mind, to warn and instruct.

Biblical Definition

To admonish is to warn and instruct, setting truth before the mind so as to turn a man from sin and folly. The Greek noutheteo joins nous, the mind, with tithemi, to place — to put a thing in someone's mind. Paul makes it the heart of his own ministry: "Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Col 1:28), where "warning" is this very word. It is first a pastoral labour: the Thessalonians are told to "know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you" (1 Thess 5:12). Yet it is not the pastor's alone, for the same letter charges the whole body, "warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thess 5:14), and Paul commends the Roman saints as "able also to admonish one another" (Rom 15:14). Admonition is therefore both an office-duty of elders and a mutual duty of the saints, always governed by love and aimed at recovery, not by harshness. This dictionary confesses admonition as an ordinary means by which Christ keeps His people, warning the unruly and instructing the wandering until every man is presented perfect in Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

To warn and instruct, placing truth before the mind to turn a man from sin. It renders the Greek noutheteo, is a pastoral duty toward the unruly, and is also commanded among all the saints toward one another.

expand to see more

ADMONISH, verb transitive. To warn and instruct; to set truth before the mind for correction.

It renders the Greek noutheteo, from nous, the mind, and is the heart of Paul's own ministry.

"Warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Col 1:28).

It is required of elders who are "over you in the Lord" (1 Thess 5:12), warning the unruly.

It is also a mutual duty of the saints, "able also to admonish one another" (Rom 15:14).

Key Scripture

Col 1:28 — "Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:"

Rom 15:14 — "And I myself also am persuaded of you, my brethren, that ye also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another."

1 Thess 5:12 — "And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you;"

1 Thess 5:14 — "Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men."

Modern Corruption

Admonition is resisted in an age that treats all warning as judgmentalism, and it is also distorted where it is severed from love and aimed at wounding rather than recovering the wanderer.

expand to see more

The spirit of the age forbids warning altogether, branding every loving rebuke as judgmental, intolerant, or unkind. But Paul makes admonition the very work of gospel ministry, "warning every man... that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Col 1:28). To withhold the warning a brother needs is not love but cruelty dressed as tolerance. The church that will not admonish abandons the unruly to their sin and forfeits an ordinary means by which Christ keeps His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is the patient, mutual character of admonition: it is to be done "in all wisdom" (Col 1:28) and with patience "toward all men" (1 Thess 5:14), by elders set over the flock and by saints toward one another. It aims always at the man's recovery, not his humiliation. A church rich in loving admonition is a church that guards its members; a church that has lost it grows soft toward sin.

Hebrew Roots

The English admonish renders the Greek noutheteo, to place in the mind, the activity of warning instruction.

expand to see more

Greek noutheteo, from nous (mind) and tithemi (to place): to put a thing in the mind.

The noun nouthesia, admonition, names the loving warning itself (Eph 6:4).

Latin admonere, to put in mind, to warn, gives our English admonish and monitor.

The word carries both warning and instruction; it confronts error and supplies truth at once.

It is governed throughout Scripture by love, patience, and the aim of recovery (1 Thess 5:14).

Usage

"He did not scold the wanderer but went to admonish him, setting Scripture plainly before his mind."

"Paul charges every saint to admonish one another, not the pastor alone."

"To admonish the unruly is an act of love, for it warns a brother off the path to ruin."
